Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette: Kwame, a 27‑year‑old African American man, spent his early childhood in a cramped house in South Carolina where his mother, a single caregiver, often resorted to harsh physical discipline. One afternoon, when he was eight, she pulled a rough, coarse blanket from a drawer and used it to wrap his arms while shouting. The tactile texture of that blanket, the sharp, uneven fibers against his skin, left a lasting imprint. In that moment, the sound of her footsteps behind him grew louder and more oppressive, the rhythm of her stride echoing like a drumbeat of impending violence. Even after the shouting stopped, the chill that settled on his forearms as she lifted the blanket lingered—a specific temperature on his skin that felt like a cold warning. Those sensory memories became triggers that would haunt him long after the house left him. In the months that followed, the mere brush of a rough cloth or the echo of a footfall would ignite a surge of alarm. He found himself hypervigilant, scanning the street for any sign of danger, his body reacting as if the threat were still present. That hypervigilance, coupled with the image of the cold blanket, led him to take increasingly risky actions—speeding through intersections, ignoring traffic signals—just to regain a sense of control. Simultaneously, the distress triggered a set of maladaptive strategies: he began to distract himself with music, to drink alcohol at the end of a long shift, and to shun intimate conversations, believing that emotional closeness would only expose him to harm. The memory of the abusive blanket also reinforced his negative appraisals: he believed he was permanently changed for the worse, that his body would never truly feel safe, and that he had lost his connection to his community. By the time he entered adulthood, those patterns had settled into a fragile routine. Driving a taxi and later an Uber, Kwame carried his past into the city streets. The texture of the worn leather seats reminded him of that rough blanket; the rumbling sound of tires on asphalt could mimic the echo of footsteps; the sudden chill of a winter wind that touched his cheeks echoed the temperature trigger from childhood. Each sensory cue instantly triggered a cascade of threat: his mind sprinted to the memory of abuse, his heart rate spiked, and he became super‑alert, convinced that danger lurked in every passerby. That threat, in turn, fueled his maladaptive strategies—he started the engine to keep the cabin warm, used distraction by playing loud music, and drank to dull the sharpness of each cold gust. The cycle also pushed him to take unnecessary risks on the road, as he sought to outrun the imagined threat, further embedding hypervigilance into his daily life. The loop tightened as each maladaptive act reinforced his negative appraisals. Avoiding intimacy meant he stayed away from coworkers and passengers alike, which deepened his sense that he had lost his community. Distraction through music and alcohol created moments where he felt detached, but each time he returned to the street, the memory of the blanket’s texture would reawaken, reintroducing the trigger. In an attempt to cope, Kwame would sometimes consume substances that made his skin feel colder, inadvertently adding a new temperature trigger to his internal list. Each time these strategies produced a fleeting sense of safety, his body still reacted with alarm, solidifying the belief that his body was an enemy, forever on guard. Now, after a series of confrontations with law enforcement over reckless driving and an incident where he nearly crashed while distracted, Kwame found himself unable to sleep, his nights filled with the echo of phantom footsteps and the rough texture of a blanket that no longer existed. He could no longer pretend that the city’s noises were harmless, and the hypervigilance that had once felt necessary now left him exhausted and isolated. It was this exhaustion, combined with the realization that his avoidance of intimacy had left him with no real support network, that finally pushed him to seek help. He came to the clinic with a heavy heart, hoping to break the cycle of fear and regain a sense of belonging, yet still terrified that the slightest touch or sound could once again send him spiraling back into the old world of hyper‑alertness and self‑harm.
